newsitem.title: GERMANY: Kohl candidacy kicks off German election campaign.
newsitem.headline: Kohl candidacy kicks off German election campaign.

text.p: Chancellor Helmut Kohl's announcement that he intends to stand for a record fifth term of office next year has kicked off Germany's general election campaign -- 18 months before voters go to the polls.

The veteran leader's comment to a television interviewer on Thursday sent waves rippling through plans for European monetary union and structural reform in Germany, hit by its worst unemployment crisis in over 60 years.

It also shifted the spotlight onto the opposition Social Democrats (SPD) -- leading the polls but undecided on their own chancellery candidate and torn between helping Kohl's reforms or trying to win votes with all-out opposition.

Kohl used an annual interview at the end of his regular 10-day Easter retreat in the Austrian Alps to end months of speculation that he did not have the stomach to lead Germany through its worst crisis since he took office in 1982.
"I will stand again because I believe I have an obligation to do this in the current situation," he said in the interview with ARD television, conducted on his 67th birthday.

The announcement was greeted with relief by his coalition partners and his own Christian Democrats (CDU), whose restlessness at Kohl's seeming lack of drive in recent months has been matched only by their fears that the old campaigner would not see them through what may be a knife-edge election.
To commentators, Kohl was throwing down the gauntlet to the SPD, which has veered between offering cooperation on reforms and sitting on the sidelines while Kohl struggles.
"In future the agenda is one of bloody conflict. Kohl's announcement has set off a marathon political election campaign," the Saarbruecker Zeitung daily said.

It may have been Kohl's reluctance to bale out with so many problems unsolved -- including post-war record unemployment of over 12 percent -- that persuaded Europe's longest serving head of government to go on after more than 14 years in office.

The mark slipped on the news because Kohl, whose name stands for European integration, is seen as the best guarantee that European monetary union will go ahead as planned in 1999 despite Germany's problems in meeting a budget deficit limit.

Those problems have to do not only with the cost of unemployment but also with Germany's slowness under Kohl to liberalise its economy and slim down its generous welfare spending to keep pace with its global competitors.
The Berliner Zeitung daily said Kohl deserved respect for staying on board as the going got tough rather than retiring to his unquestioned place in history.
But it said his decision was "both the best thing and the worst thing that could happen to his party".
"With Kohl, it has a good chance of election success and forces the SPD to make radical leadership choices. But Kohl's new candidacy will prevent overdue reforms taking place..."

Kohl's system of rule by consensus has come under a harsh spotlight this year as belated proposals to reform the tax and pensions systems have only unsettled voters who find it hard in the current climate to see beyond job losses and benefit cuts.
But the master tactician may be gambling on the SPD doing no better when forced to nail its own colours to the mast.

So far, the SPD has succeeded in putting off its choice of chancellery candidate -- a two-horse race between left-leaning party leader Oskar Lafontaine and the more business-friendly Lower Saxony premier Gerhard Schroeder, who polls say has a much better chance against Kohl.
The pressure to decide is now sure to mount, and Kohl knows the SPD has a long history of tearing itself apart in personal squabbles while he reaps the spoils.
